clue.text: Criticise notice displayed after a game

indicators.note: the notice is shown following the game, so it comes second in the answer

parts.note: nim is an old game of taking matchsticks from piles
an advert is a public notice

explanation.surface: Someone is criticised by a notice put up after a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' is the old matchstick game; 'displayed after' tells you the notice comes last, behind the A and the game.
explanation.definitionFit: To animadvert is a formal verb for passing censure or adverse comment.

clue.text: Simpleton, silly old one

indicators.note: silly suggests the letters of the words behave foolishly and get jumbled

explanation.surface: An old person is called a silly simpleton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'silly' rearranges the six letters of OLD ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A noodle is an old informal word for a fool or dimwit.

clue.text: False alarm important? Nonsense!

indicators.note: something false is not genuine, so these letters are not in their true order

parts.note: key means crucial or important

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a false alarm as important, calling it rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'False' reads as describing the alarm, but it is the anagram signal; the shuffled letters come out as MALAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Malarkey is slang for meaningless talk or humbug, said as an exclamation of disbelief.

clue.text: Face up to pupils I kept in, or release from restriction?

indicators.note: the pupils and the I are kept inside the word for confronting, like children held back after school

parts.note: to defy is to confront or face up to
a class is a group of pupils

explanation.surface: A teacher wonders whether to confront the pupils held in detention or to let them go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kept in' suggests school detention but is the container signal, splitting the verb for confronting around the class and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Declassifying secret documents frees them from official restrictions on who may see them.

clue.text: Reveal Brussels fraud? That sounds good

parts.note: Brussels is the seat of the EU, the European Union
a phony is a fraud or impostor

explanation.surface: Exposing fraud at the European Union in Brussels would be welcome news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reveal' is surface colour: the pieces are EU and PHONY, and the definition plays on the surface's 'That sounds good' as approval.
explanation.definitionFit: Euphony means pleasing harmony of sound, so a euphonious thing sounds pleasant.

clue.text: Dog getting a few rabbits

definitions.meaning: to dog someone is to follow them closely, to shadow them
in cricket, poor batsmen are rabbits, and the weak batters at the end of the order are collectively called this

explanation.surface: A dog catches a handful of bunnies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rabbits' is cricket slang for hopeless batsmen, who bat at the end of a team's order; that end is so named.
explanation.definitionFit: Following someone closely is shadowing them, and in cricket the lower-order batters form the batting order's end.

clue.text: Artist entered privately

parts.note: entered means came in, written as two words
RA, a Royal Academician, is a standard abbreviation for an artist

explanation.surface: An artist went in without being seen.
explanation.walkthrough: IN CAME (entered) then RA; the answer is the legal phrase for a hearing closed to the public.
explanation.definitionFit: A case heard in camera is held in a judge's private rooms, away from the public.

clue.text: Needlework that produces lumbar pain?

parts.note: reads as a sewing technique whose name, taken literally, is a sharp pain in the lower back

explanation.surface: Bending over sewing gives someone a sore lower back.
explanation.definitionFit: This sewing stitch overlaps each new stitch backwards on the previous one, and its name also suggests a twinge in the lumbar region.

clue.text: She shows alarm — left, right, and centre

indicators.note: the left-hand end of the word alarm supplies its first letter
the right-hand end of the word alarm supplies its last letter

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the centre of the five-letter word alarm is its third letter

explanation.surface: A woman displays panic in every direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left, right, and centre' looks like 'everywhere', but the three positions pick letters from ALARM: left A, right M, then the word AND, then the centre A.
explanation.definitionFit: Amanda is a woman's given name, which 'She' stands for.

clue.text: It prevents a daft head being exposed in the paper

definitions.text: It prevents a daft head being exposed in the paper

parts.words: It prevents a daft head being exposed in the paper
parts.note: reads as headgear for a jester covering a silly head, and also names a size of writing paper

explanation.surface: Something stops a silly person's head showing up in the press.
explanation.definitionFit: This large paper size took its name from the jester's-hat watermark once used on it.

clue.text: Sign of excellence in husband everyone notices

parts.note: all means everyone
to mark is to notice

explanation.surface: A wife's husband stands out because everyone notices him.
explanation.definitionFit: A hallmark is the stamp of quality on precious metal, and so any distinguishing mark of quality.

clue.text: One way to cure a spasmodic twitch

definitions.meaning: ... meat preserves it by drying it in strips
a sudden involuntary jolt of a muscle

explanation.surface: A remedy is sought for a nervous tic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cure' looks medical, but it is curing meat, as in jerky.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat is preserved by drying in strips this way, and a sudden muscle spasm has the same name.

clue.text: Distribution of post patient person's running

parts.note: Job, the Biblical figure, is the byword for patience
haring means running fast, like a hare

explanation.surface: The way mail is shared out depends on a patient person dashing about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'post' means a job here, not mail.
explanation.definitionFit: Two part-time workers splitting one position divide that post between them.

clue.text: Most refined habits appropriate for those going into service

definitions.text: Most refined habits appropriate for those going into service

parts.words: Most refined habits appropriate for those going into service
parts.note: reads as finest clothing suitable for people attending a church service, habits meaning garments

explanation.surface: The finest conduct suits people entering domestic service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'habits' suggests behaviour and 'service' employment; here they are clothes and church.
explanation.definitionFit: One's finest clothes were traditionally kept for wearing to church at the weekend.

clue.text: Sportsman in real disarray, left before taking part in fight

indicators.note: the jumbled letters take in the following pieces, holding them inside
letters in disarray are thrown out of order
left comes ahead of the next piece in the answer

parts.note: a round is one section of a boxing bout

explanation.surface: A sportsman in a mess walks out before joining a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disarray' jumbles the four letters of 'real' to ALER; 'taking' has it swallow the left-plus-round pair after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A player skilled at both batting and bowling, or across many disciplines, is called this.

clue.text: Accept responsibility for a small charge

definitions.text: Accept responsibility for a small charge

parts.words: Accept responsibility for a small charge
parts.note: reads as taking on a minor fee or offence, but means looking after a little child in one's care

explanation.surface: Someone owns up to a minor accusation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charge' suggests a fee or accusation; here it is a child in one's care.
explanation.definitionFit: Minding a young child while the parents are out is looking after one's little ward.

clue.text: They may give Cockney a ring on his birthday

definitions.text: They may give Cockney a ring on his birthday

parts.words: They may give Cockney a ring on his birthday
parts.note: reads as friends phoning a Londoner on his birthday, but means church bells heard at his birth

explanation.surface: Friends might phone a Londoner to wish him happy birthday.
explanation.walkthrough: A true Cockney is traditionally born within the sound of the bells of St Mary-le-Bow church in east London; 'ring' and 'birthday' point to that.
explanation.definitionFit: The bells of St Mary-le-Bow define Cockney birth: being born within earshot of them.

clue.text: Experienced hand that's spent too much time in the cellar?

definitions.text: Experienced hand that's spent too much time in the cellar?

parts.words: Experienced hand that's spent too much time in the cellar?
parts.note: reads as an aged seasoning left in a salt cellar, but means a veteran sailor, a hand being a crew member

explanation.surface: A seasoned worker has been down in the wine cellar too long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cellar' suggests wine, but a salt cellar is a table pot for salt; 'hand' is a ship's crewman.
explanation.definitionFit: A seasoned, long-serving sailor is so called, a hand being a member of a ship's crew.

clue.text: Butcher's disorganised — he left work unfinished

indicators.note: disorganised letters are in no proper order and must be sorted out

parts.note: the eight letters of the word with its s

explanation.surface: A slapdash butcher walks off leaving the job half done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disorganised' rearranges BUTCHERS. 'work unfinished' alludes to the composer's Unfinished Symphony.
explanation.definitionFit: The Austrian composer's Eighth Symphony is famously known as the Unfinished.

clue.text: Short of fare to go round a European country

indicators.note: the word for lacking food encircles the single letter

parts.note: someone short of food is hungry, fare meaning food

explanation.surface: Someone lacking money for food tours a country in Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fare' suggests a ticket price but means food; 'to go round' puts A inside HUNGRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Hungary is a landlocked state in central Europe.

clue.text: Greeting in an awkward situation

definitions.meaning: a formal salutation on being introduced
a fine mess or commotion, as in 'a fine how-d'ye-do'

explanation.surface: Someone says hello at an embarrassing moment.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a formal salutation and also, informally, a predicament or fuss.

clue.text: Off. Oxford Street

definitions.meaning: meat or game that is off is going bad, ripe-smelling
the main street of Oxford is known simply by this name, with 'the'

explanation.surface: Turn off Oxford Street, a London shopping road.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxford Street suggests London's shopping street; here it is the main street in the city of Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: Tainted, smelly meat is so described, and Oxford's principal road is called the ___ Street.

clue.text: Frenchman imprisoned by hearing as conspirator

indicators.note: the letters are held captive inside the run of words that follow

explanation.surface: A Frenchman is jailed after the hearing finds him a plotter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'imprisoned by' signals letters sitting inside 'hearing as conspirator'.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Gascony in south-west France; d'Artagnan is the famous example.

clue.text: Wine that's taken by king with sweet drink

indicators.note: the abbreviation for 'that is' is taken by the king, coming after it

parts.note: R, from Latin rex, is the standard abbreviation for king
i.e., Latin id est, means 'that is'
a sling is a sweetened spirit-based cocktail, as in Singapore sling

explanation.surface: Wine accepted by a monarch along with a sugary cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's' is the Latin abbreviation id est; 'taken by' puts it after the king, with the cocktail following.
explanation.definitionFit: Riesling is a white grape variety and the wine made from it, notably in Germany.

clue.text: A number of locals, perhaps, forming popular partnership

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
North and South form a partnership at the bridge table

explanation.surface: Local residents join together in a well-liked alliance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'locals' are pubs, a British word for one's neighbourhood pub.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain one's 'local' is one's regular pub, so several pubs are a number of these.

clue.text: Interview people in TV studio, perhaps

definitions.meaning: a formal meeting with a monarch or pope, granted to a visitor

explanation.surface: Guests in a television studio are interviewed.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal meeting with a dignitary and a body of spectators both carry this name.

clue.text: Hold with both arms? Not always

definitions.text: Hold with both arms? Not always

parts.words: Hold with both arms? Not always
parts.note: reads as a wrestling grip using both arms, and also hints at the one-armed British admiral

explanation.surface: Someone is told to grip with both arms, though not every time.
explanation.walkthrough: A full version of this wrestling hold uses both arms, a half version one; the famous admiral lost his right arm.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a wrestling hold applied under the opponent's arms, and Britain's most famous admiral, who lost an arm.

clue.text: Form of advertising that involves high-fliers with smoking?

definitions.text: Form of advertising that involves high-fliers with smoking?

parts.words: Form of advertising that involves high-fliers with smoking?
parts.note: reads as executives promoting cigarettes, but means pilots trailing smoke to spell messages in the air

explanation.surface: An advertising campaign has top executives promoting cigarettes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high-fliers' suggests ambitious executives but means pilots; 'smoking' is their aircraft's smoke trail.
explanation.definitionFit: Aircraft trail smoke to trace letters across the heavens as aerial advertising.
